content: Hemp oil is derived from the seeds of the hemp plant, which contain approximately 30-35% oil by weight. This oil is particularly rich in essential fatty acids. The oil can be extracted by pressing the seeds, and when cold-pressed and unrefined, it has a light green color with a nutty and grassy flavor. In contrast, refined hemp oil is clear and has minimal flavor. Hemp oil is widely utilized in various applications, including body care products, lubricants, paints, and industrial uses. Its antimicrobial properties make it a valuable ingredient in soaps, shampoos, and detergents. Nutritionally, hemp oil is highly regarded due to its 3:1 ratio of omega-6 to omega-3 essential fatty acids, which aligns with the balance required by the human body. In recent years, it has also gained attention as a potential source of biodiesel. Hemp oil is specifically manufactured to contain negligible amounts of THC, the psychoactive compound in cannabis, and is therefore not considered a psychoactive drug. Approximately 30-35% of the weight of hemp seeds is composed of oil, which contains 80% essential fatty acids (EFAs). These include linoleic acid (LA) at 50-70%, alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) at 15-25%, and gamma-linolenic acid (GLA) at 1-6%. The proportions of linoleic acid and alpha-linolenic acid in hemp seed oil meet the human body's requirements for EFAs. However, the high unsaturated fat content of hemp oil makes it prone to becoming rancid quickly unless stored in dark-colored bottles or combined with chemical preservatives. This characteristic complicates its transportation and storage. Additionally, the high unsaturated fat content renders hemp oil unsuitable for frying, as cooking with it reduces its nutritional value and may transform beneficial fatty acids into less favorable substances. These limitations significantly restrict hemp oil's potential in the food market, although it retains some marketing potential as a nutritional supplement.
